newsitem.title: INDIA: India offers reward for news on Kashmir hostages.
newsitem.headline: India offers reward for news on Kashmir hostages.

text.p: Indian police on Friday released handbills announcing a reward of up to one million rupees ($28,000) for information on four Western tourists taken captive in Kashmir 17 months ago.

The posters featured pictures of American Donald Hutchings, German Dirk Hasert and Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells, who were kidnapped by shadowy Al-Faran separatist militants in troubled Jammu and Kashmir state in July 1995.
One other hostage, American John Childs, escaped, while a sixth, Hans Christian Ostroe of Norway, was found beheaded in August 1995.
The handbill said the four Westerners remained untraced.

"The state government of Jammu and Kashmir announces a reward up to one million rupees to any person/persons who provides specific information about (the hostages) location in whatever state/condition," it said.
It said the identity of the informer would be kept confidential.
The notice listed phone numbers in Srinagar and Jammu, respectively the summer and winter capitals of Jammu and Kashmir state, as well as in Delhi.
It also provided post office box numbers in Srinagar and Jammu.

In a separate statement, state police said there had not been any reliable reports of sightings of the four hostages since the end of November 1995, when negotiations between Indian officials and Al-Faran broke down.
Local Kashmiris have periodically reported sighting the four remaining hostages, but authorities have been unable to determine with certainty whether the captives are dead or alive.
The statement said family members of the hostages had visited the state and experienced "severe trauma".

U.S. diplomats said in October they hoped to tap a government programme that offers up to $2 million for information that can be used to combat acts of "terrorism" aimed at citizens abroad for a reward for news of the hostages.
Indian authorities opposed allowing the United States to offer the reward in India.
The police statement said the rewards aimed to secure "the cooperation of the people at large in being able to locate and reach the hostages, wherever they be, and in whatever condition".
Al-Faran had not been heard of before the kidnappings. Dozens of guerrilla groups are fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir, the predominantly Hindu nation's only Moslem majority state.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have died in the six-year-old revolt.
